newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president visits south, students protest.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president visits south, students protest.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Wednesday travelled to the southern town of Gjirokaster, gauging the public mood in the wake of mass fury against pyramid investment swindles.

The president, who must seek a fresh term of office in a vote in parliament by March 9, has told supporters during a 10-day nationwide tour that his ruling Democrats are partly to blame for tolerating the collapsed investment schemes.

But Berisha, elected on a pro-market ticket in 1992, said the main responsibility lay with gullible investors and he has refused to bail out the companies by printing money to compensate thousands of people facing ruin.
Students in Albania's southernmost town of Gjirokaster, near the Greek border, said on Wednesday they were boycotting classes indefinitely in protest against the financial scandal.

Street-cleaning vehicles were at work in front of the sports hall where Berisha was expected to address supporters later on Wednesday. Security was tight, with police preventing people from walking near the building.
Some 970 students mounted their boycott in solidarity with student hunger strikers in the southern town of Vlore, where protesters have staged peaceful daily marches for three weeks.
"No discos, no walks, no bars. Let us stay here from morning until evening," a student spokesman said.
Student leaders said they would refuse to speak to Berisha, who on Tuesday offered to open a dialogue with the growing number of university protesters across the country.
Police were paying close attention to student activities after weeks of sporadic but violent protests sparked by the collapse of five fraudulent investment funds.
Hundreds of thousands of people in Europe's poorest state have lost much of their savings by pouring all they had into funds which promised interest of up to 60 percent a month.
In the capital Tirana on Tuesday, plain-clothes police stopped students from organising a peaceful demonstration on their own campus.

The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday it was increasingly worried that the Albanian authorities were preventing peaceful protests from taking place. It was also concerned about reported beatings of opposition members and journalists.
Washington repeated its call for a new constitution and fresh general elections after last May's nationwide poll, which it has described as "seriously flawed".
The U.S. ambassador in Tirana, Marisa Lino has called for political parties to begin a serious dialogue over the Balkan state's future.

"The process of compiling a new constitution would lay the basis for fresh elections, which is what we have been saying during the past nine months," Lino told the independent daily Koha Jone in an interview.

Lino said she had no immediate plans to attend parliament next week for voting to elect a president. Berisha is widely expected to be given a new five-year mandate as the assembly is dominated by his right-wing Democratic Party.

The European Union on Monday offered Albania help to get its economy and financial institutions in order, but only if Tirana works closely with the International Monetary Fund. It insisted the government also had to stick to democratic principles.
